title: Levy-Based Framework Most Likely to Meet IMO Emissions Checkpoints: IMarEST
summary: IMarEST's analysis for the IMO identifies a levy-based framework as the most likely path to meet 2030 and 2040 emissions checkpoints, proposing fixed financial penalties for non-compliant ships. Yet, the suggestion that the current Net-Zero Framework could offer the lowest abatement cost relies on the dubious premise of stable biofuel prices until 2038, a significant greenwashing risk. Without immediate, concrete financial disincentives for high-emitting vessels, these discussions remain largely theoretical, allowing continued reliance on heavy fuel oil.
content:
IMarEST submits comparative analysis of all four NZF options to the IMO

Levy-based framework most likely to deliver 2030 and 2040 emissions checkpoints, analysis finds

Current-form NZF could offer lowest average abatement cost if biofuel prices stay in check

Industry consultation on IMO GHG measures open until September 16

The Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) has submitted a series of papers to the IMO comparing the four proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF) options side by side for the first time.

The submissions come ahead of the 22nd Intersessional Working Group on GHG Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 22), which meets from September 1-4 as member states work towards agreement on a framework for international shipping.

The analysis evaluates each of the four proposed MARPOL amendment options against the emissions goals of the IMO's 2023 GHG Strategy, and finds a levy-based framework is most likely to deliver the 2030 and 2040 emissions reduction checkpoints.

That option proposes fixed financial penalties for vessels not complying with emissions standards, with subsidies reserved for operators using zero or near-zero emission fuels and technologies.

However, the study also finds that keeping the NZF in its current form could offer the lowest average carbon abatement cost among the pricing-based options, provided significant increases in biofuel prices are avoided before 2038.

The work draws on modelling by University College London's Energy Institute Shipping and Oceans Research Group and the Rocky Mountain Institute.

"This is the first study to model the specifics of all four proposals side-by-side, building on the assumptions and methods used in the IMO's own Comprehensive Impact Assessment of mid-term measures," Dr Tristan Smith, professor of energy and transport at UCL's Energy Institute and head of the IMarEST IMO GHG delegation, said in a statement.

"As negotiations intensify ahead of MEPC 85 at the end of the year, we are hopeful our analysis will help guide IMO member states to a workable solution for the Net-Zero Framework."

The institute has also launched an industry consultation on the effectiveness of current IMO GHG measures, open until September 16 to individuals and organisations with a stake in maritime decarbonisation.

title: UK Targets Arctic LNG Carrier, Five Oil Tankers in Latest Russia Sanctions Package
summary: The UK has sanctioned six vessels, including LNG carrier Arctic Express (IMO 9333591) and five oil tankers, for transporting Russian energy exports. These vessels, often sailing under flags of convenience, now face port bans and severe restrictions on maritime services. Such operations, frequently lacking transparency, raise serious questions about their actual carbon intensity, unchecked HFO usage, and compliance with global environmental standards.
content:
The United Kingdom has expanded its sanctions against Russia with a new package targeting shipping, banking, and industrial entities, including six vessels accused of transporting Russian energy exports and an India-based ship management company.

In a sanctions notice issued Thursday, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office announced 19 new designations under its Russia sanctions regime, adding ships, companies, banks, and an individual to the UK sanctions list.

The maritime measures are led by the designation of the LNG carrier Arctic Express (IMO 9333591), which the UK says has transported liquefied natural gas originating in Russia to third countries. The vessel, currently believed to be sailing under the Russian flag, is operated by SMP Tech Management LLP.

Also designated is Frion Ship Management LLP, a Mumbai-based ship management company that the UK alleges supported the sale of the Arctic Express into Russian ownership and control. The company is now subject to an asset freeze, trust services restrictions, director disqualification measures, and transport sanctions.

The UK also imposed shipping sanctions on five oil tankers that it says have carried Russian crude oil or petroleum products from Russia to third countries:

Perseas (IMO 9326811), believed to be sailing under the San Marino flag.

Torvian (IMO 9470131), believed to be registered in Barbados.

Asteras (IMO 9402263), believed to be registered in Palau.

Visund (IMO 9378864), believed to be registered in Palau.

Zenturo (IMO 9346885), believed to be registered in Barbados.

Under the UK’s specified ship sanctions, the vessels are prohibited from entering UK ports, may be detained, cannot be chartered or operated by UK persons, and are subject to restrictions on a wide range of maritime services, including chartering, brokering, technical assistance, financial services, and crew services.

Beyond the shipping sector, the sanctions package includes Northern Engineering LLC, which the UK says operates in Russia’s strategically significant energy sector, four industrial companies accused of supplying goods or technology supporting Russia’s war effort, and five Russian financial institutions, including Ozon Bank and the Russian Export-Import Bank, which face asset freezes and correspondent banking restrictions.

The latest measures underscore the UK’s continued focus on disrupting the maritime networks that facilitate Russian energy exports. Since the invasion of Ukraine, London has increasingly used shipping-specific sanctions to target vessels, operators, and service providers involved in transporting Russian oil and LNG to global markets.

title: PortXchange joins SASHA Coalition, bringing port emissions and operational insight
summary: PortXchange has joined the SASHA Coalition, aiming to integrate port operational realities into zero-emission shipping policies and infrastructure discussions. While advocating for port perspectives is necessary, such coalitions often generate more rhetoric than tangible carbon reduction, leaving high-emitting vessels largely unchecked. The industry urgently requires concrete, verifiable actions to reduce CO2 emissions and HFO consumption, not just another discussion forum while ships continue to exceed their CII ratings.
content:
22

Maritime technology company joins coalition to ensure port data, infrastructure and operational realities help shape the transition to zero-emission shipping

(ROTTERDAM, Netherlands, 6 August 2026) — PortXchange has joined the SASHA Coalition as its first member focused on port emissions and operational intelligence.

The SASHA Coalition is an industry alliance that brings together companies developing the most sustainable shipping and aviation energy systems, including those based on renewable hydrogen and zero-emission technologies, to advocate for supportive policy.

PortXchange will work with the coalition to ensure that ports have a seat at the table on policy, funding and infrastructure decisions, not a briefing after those decisions are made.

PortXchange maintained that ports are where new fuels are delivered, infrastructure is built and the energy transition either works, or it doesn’t. That piece is too often missing from the conversation.

“Ports’ potential to drive climate action has been largely overlooked,” states Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director & Co-Founder, PortXchange. “We will not achieve the emissions reductions needed, at the pace required, until all the actors across the value chain collaborate. That is why PortXchange is joining the SASHA Coalition: to bring the port perspective into the conversation and help turn zero-emission ambition into action.

“Cleaner fuels are essential, but producing them is only half the job. The transition has to work when it reaches the port. That means understanding where future demand is likely to emerge, where infrastructure will have the greatest impact and how those investments fit with real port operations.

“Ports are where vessels, fuels, infrastructure, cargo and communities meet. If the port perspective is missing, we risk building an energy transition that looks convincing on paper but struggles in practice.

”Sabrina Khan-Dighe, Membership & Advocacy Officer at the SASHA Coalition, said: “We will only see shipping on track for net zero when all actors are working together across the sector, and ports’ importance as a key to unlocking cross-sector decarbonisation cannot be overstated. Developing cleaner fuels and technologies is critical, but adoption will depend on ports having the right infrastructure and operational readiness to support investment.”

“We’re thrilled to have PortXchange join the SASHA Coalition and add its voice to the increasing number of innovative companies calling for regulatory changes to help them thrive.”

PortXchange’s EmissionInsider platform gives ports visibility across emissions from ships, trucks, rail and terminal activity. It helps users identify hotspots, evaluate reduction measures, plan infrastructure and turn emissions data into better-informed investment decisions.

That is the gap PortXchange will work with the SASHA Coalition to close. Clean-fuel infrastructure decisions cannot run on ambition alone. They need credible data on vessel activity, operational patterns and where investment will deliver the greatest impact.

“There is a tendency in maritime decarbonization to jump straight to the future fuel and assume the rest will fall into place,” de Jager continued. “It will not. Infrastructure, demand, operational readiness and policy have to move together.

“And while we prepare for tomorrow’s fuels, we cannot ignore today’s emissions. Ports do not have the luxury of waiting for one perfect technology to arrive. They need to understand their emissions now, act on the sources they can influence and make better investment decisions for what comes next. That is the perspective we are bringing to SASHA.”

Through the coalition, PortXchange will push for zero-emission shipping policy that treats ports as active participants in the transition, not simply the places expected to make everyone else’s plans work.

title: Seaspan Energy opportunities are multiplying with commercial shipping’s quest for lower-carbon fuel alternatives
summary: Seaspan Energy touts its 150th ship-to-ship LNG bunkering as a "lower-carbon" fuel opportunity, yet this fossil gas solution presents significant methane slip challenges. Such incremental steps offer only marginal improvements to fleet carbon intensity, potentially risking future FuelEU Maritime fines for major operators like Seaspan Corp. Genuine decarbonization demands more than transitioning between fossil fuels, especially for a fleet with 2.4 million TEU capacity.
content:
B.C. as an alternative energy fuelling hub for transpacific maritime shipping?

Another flight of fantasy, you say, in David Eby’s NDP land of pipeline opposition escalation, private property rights erosion, and government debt accumulation acceleration?

Maybe not.

Maybe we have more facts than fantasy to consider on that file.

Here is one: Seaspan Energy (SE).

The North Vancouver-based member of the Seaspan Marine group of companies recently announced that it had completed its 150th ship-to-ship liquefied natural gas bunkering. That would be 150 in under two years since SE launched its operations; that would also be enough to nail down seventh overall in Lansdowne Moritz’s LNG bunkering volume rankings.

Granted, not top five; however, not bad.

Even better when you consider that when SE’s Seaspan Lions refuelled a tanker with LNG in the Port of Vancouver on Jan. 30, 2025, it was Canada’s first ship-to-ship LNG bunkering operation.

That entrepreneurial spirit is typical of companies aligned with the Washington Group, which has launched such major maritime business success stories as Seaspan Corp., the world’s largest independent lessor of container ships.

Seaspan Corp., as avid Substack Shipping News (SSN) readers might recall, acquired APR Energy Ltd. in an all-stock transaction valued at US$750 million in 2020 as part of Seaspan’s plan to diversify into the energy sector.

At the time, APR was the world’s largest lessor of mobile gas turbines. Seaspan, which had undergone a major corporate retooling that included launching Atlas Corp. as its corporate parent, was later taken private and acquired by the Poseidon Acquisition Corp. in an all-cash US$11 billion deal.

Seaspan’s container ship fleet today numbers 227 – 890 per cent more than it started with in the early 21st century. The company’s overall capacity is now around 2.4 million 20-foot equivalent units (TEU).

All of which is to illustrate the global ambitions of Seaspan companies.

So, a seventh overall ship-to-ship LNG bunkering rank today will not remain seventh for long.

Bet on SE’s fleet of three LNG bunkering ships expanding with the demand for dual-fuel ships as maritime shipping’s pollution restrictions tighten and carbon emissions penalties erode earnings.

Still, today’s dual-fuel ship market remains marginally buoyant.

As noted in a previous SSN report, orders for alternative-fuel ships in 2026’s first half dropped to 137 compared with 155 in 2025’s first six months and were down 45 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024.

Concerns over fuel availability, regulatory uncertainty, and comparative cost have dampened demand for dual-fuel ships.

However, A.P. Moller-Maersk (CPH:MAERSK-B) and other top ocean carrier lines remain committed to increasing their fleets’ energy efficiency and reducing their carbon footprints.

And LNG remains the odds-on favourite lower-carbon emission bridge fuel to a greener maritime shipping future.

As the World Bank Group (WBG) points out in its recently released “Ports, Ships, and Fuels” report, “LNG is currently the most widely deployed alternative marine fuel, with approximately 470 LNG-fueled ships in service globally and more than 400 on order – well ahead of other alternatives.”

Well ahead by a wide margin.

Yang Chen, the managing director and chief editor of Xinde Marine News, points out in a recent analysis that 173 LNG-capable ships were ordered in 2026’s first half compared with only four methanol ships.

Bets on which bridge fuel will drive ocean carriers to the industry’s green destination are multibillion-dollar gambles.

Bunker fuel typically represents 40 per cent to 60 per cent of a ship’s operating budget, and a 10,000 TEU container ship costs approximately US$100 million and has a working life of around 25 years.

The supporting infrastructure for that fuel bridge is critical to its commercial viability.

So, whoever is pushing chips into the middle of the table needs to be confident that he is making an informed bet.

Again, LNG has the inside track.

The WBG report estimates “that by 2040, supporting global maritime fuel supply could require about US$310 billion for green ammonia, US$81 billion for green methanol, and US$42 billion for renewable LNG.”

It focuses on the Pacific region and notes that China is leading the push to dominate green shipping initiatives.

The report says, for example, that the shipbuilding action plan for China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has an international market share target of more than 50 per cent for green-powered vessels.

“Complementary measures include large-scale LNG bunkering infrastructure at ports such as Yangshan and Yantian and coordinated institutional support through state-owned enterprises.”

B.C. cannot hope to win any head-to-head industrial competition with China; however, its natural resource and geographic advantages could establish it as a player in the transpacific shipping theatre.

It just needs the private-sector mettle and government commitment to leverage those advantages.

Seaspan provides evidence that the West Coast still has that mettle; British Columbians await any sign that their government has the required commitment.

This article originally appeared in The Substack Shipping News. Timothy Renshaw can be reached at [email protected].

title: Peninsula and Evos Sign MOU to Develop Biofuel Storage Infrastructure in the Port of Algeciras
summary: Peninsula and Evos plan 60,000 m3 of biofuel storage in Algeciras, positioning this "versatile" fuel as a convenient answer to impending FuelEU Maritime regulations. This proposed infrastructure, driven by "price volatility" and regulatory pressure, remains a plan offering no immediate reduction in current carbon intensity or excessive HFO usage. True decarbonization demands immediate, verifiable emission cuts and improved CII ratings, not merely future "green" infrastructure to mitigate fines.
content:
Peninsula, the world’s leading hybrid marine fuels supplier, and Evos, a European independent liquid energy and chemicals storage company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to jointly progress the development of dedicated biofuel storage infrastructure at Evos’ terminal in the Port of Algeciras.

The proposed Evos expansion includes plans to develop up to 60,000 cubic metres of storage capacity, fully allocated to Peninsula to support the expansion of its biofuels supply chain in the region.

Located at the Strait of Gibraltar—one of the world’s busiest maritime corridors—the Evos Algeciras expansion project is intended to strengthen infrastructure for the energy transition in shipping. It will provide dedicated storage and handling capacity for low-carbon marine fuels, underpinning Peninsula’s quality proposition through control of its own supply chain.

John A. Bassadone, founder and CEO of Peninsula commented: “We are seeing an acceleration of biofuel adoption as a result of price volatility of conventional fuels and regulatory measures such as FuelEU and EU ETS. These regulations are designed to ratchet up, and biofuels are the most versatile, available option today to meet decarbonisation targets. By partnering with Evos to build storage infrastructure, it allows us to control the quality of product and to blend biofuel ratios according to market demand. It will also offer our customers full flexibility and optionality when lifting bio products from us and further demonstrates Peninsula’s active commitment to the decarbonisation of marine fuels.”

Under the MOU, the parties will continue technical and commercial discussions on a long-term storage and handling agreement, subject to Evos’ final investment decision.

Evos will lead project development at its Algeciras terminal, including engineering, permitting and construction, while Peninsula will integrate the capacity into its growing global biofuels supply network.

Daan Vos, CEO at Evos, commented: “Algeciras is already an important bunker and trading hub, with direct relevance to global shipping activity and inter-Mediterranean trade flows. Evos has a well-established position in the port as a bunker fuel storage terminal, and the expansion project with a strategic partner such as Peninsula builds on that position. By developing infrastructure for marine biofuels, we can respond to changing demand in the bunker market and strengthen Algeciras’ role in the transition to lower-carbon shipping.”

title: CNOOC's LNG Vessel Named Greenergy River
summary: NYK and CNOOC's joint venture, HLT, has named its new LNG carrier "GREENERGY RIVER", a dubious moniker for a vessel still relying on fossil fuels. Despite claims of "state-of-the-art dual-fuel engines" utilizing boil-off gas, the vessel will still burn fuel oil, and LNG's significant methane slip often undermines its purported carbon intensity benefits. dirtiestships.com will monitor "GREENERGY RIVER"'s operational emissions data to assess if its environmental impact truly aligns with its 'greenergy' branding, or if it's merely another exercise in greenwashing.
content:
Yesterday HUAJING LNG TRANSPORT PTE. LTD. (HLT), a joint venture company in which NYK participates, held a naming ceremony for a new liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier for the CNOOC Group, a Chinese state-owned energy company.

The ceremony took place at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding (Group) Co., Ltd. in China, where the vessel is being built, and the ship was named “GREENERGY RIVER.” The ceremony was attended by NYK Senior Managing Executive Officer Hironobu Watanabe and other related parties.

HLT is a joint venture company comprising NYK; CNOOC Gas and Power Singapore Trading & Marketing Pte. Ltd. (CNOOC SG), a subsidiary of the CNOOC Group; CETS Investment Management (HK) Co., Ltd. (CETS); and CMES LNG Project 4 Company Limited, a subsidiary of China Merchants Energy Shipping Co., Ltd. (CMES), a major Chinese shipping company.

GREENERGY RIVER is the first of a series of six LNG carriers that HLT will deploy for CNOOC SG under this project. It is also the first China-built LNG carrier involving NYK to be deployed under a long-term charter contract with a Chinese customer. From August, the ship is scheduled to transport LNG procured by the CNOOC Group from suppliers worldwide primarily to China. The vessel will be managed by OPearl LNG Ship Management Company Limited, a ship-management company established jointly by NYK, CMES, and CETS.

The ship is equipped with a highly fuel-efficient, state-of-the-art dual-fuel engine that uses fuel oil and boil-off gas (LNG vaporized in cargo tanks during navigation) as fuel. This system enable efficient navigation, contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and help lower the ship’s environmental impact.

title: Anew Climate joins SEA-LNG
summary: Anew Climate, a self-proclaimed 'low-carbon fuels leader', has joined the SEA-LNG coalition, promoting its "methane decarbonisation pathway" via liquefied biomethane (Bio-LNG). While claiming up to 80% GHG reduction, the actual well-to-wake impact and scalability of Bio-LNG remain dubious, especially as it primarily offers FuelEU Maritime compliance credits. This engagement appears more focused on leveraging existing LNG infrastructure and financial incentives than driving the urgent, substantial carbon intensity reductions required from dirty ships.
content:
Anew Climate, a global leader in low-carbon fuels and climate solutions, has joined the SEA-LNG coalition. Anew’s support will boost SEA-LNG’s work to reduce emissions across the global shipping industry by promoting the adoption of the methane decarbonisation pathway.

Majority-owned by TPG Rise, Anew delivers liquefied biomethane (LBM or Bio-LNG) for maritime decarbonisation across vital shipping hubs in North America, Europe, and Asia, reducing GHG emissions by up to 80% compared to marine diesel on a full well-to-wake basis.

Anew’s membership in SEA-LNG comes as liquefied biomethane adoption accelerates under regulations like FuelEU Maritime, which requires fleet operators to pool to meet GHG intensity targets. Liquefied biomethane use generates credits within this pooling mechanism, which operators can use directly for compliance or sell to other fleet operators. Liquefied biomethane leverages existing LNG infrastructure and is already bunkered at roughly 70 ports across Europe, the U.S., and parts of Asia. Some pathways can achieve negative carbon intensity by avoiding emissions, such as methane that would otherwise be released from waste streams.

Andy Brosnan, President of Low Carbon Fuels, Anew Climate, said: “Bio-LNG is one of the most practical and scalable tools available today to help the maritime sector reduce emissions and meet evolving regulatory requirements. We’re seeing growing momentum across global shipping as stakeholders turn decarbonisation commitments into action. Through SEA-LNG, we look forward to collaborating with industry leaders to accelerate the availability and adoption of Bio-LNG and support the industry’s transition to lower-carbon fuels.”

Steve Esau, COO of SEA-LNG, added: “Anew’s membership expands our North American footprint and supports the methane decarbonisation pathway’s global expansion. As a first mover in bringing liquefied biomethane to scale, Anew joins a roster of fuel producers with a proven track record, a presence in strategic shipping hubs, and a tangible impact on compliance and decarbonisation today.”

title: Integrated Maritime Ecosystems: The Next Frontier of the Blue Economy
summary: The maritime industry's latest "profound transformation" narrative promises "sustainable growth" and "resilient ecosystems" on its path to IMO 2050 net-zero. This high-level rhetoric, however, conveniently sidesteps the reality that global shipping emissions could still increase by 50% by 2050. Without immediate, tangible strategies to curb carbon intensity, such "industrial transformations" remain mere greenwashing, inviting future FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
Image Source: Getty Images

This is part of the essay series: Sagarmanthan Edit 2026.

The maritime industry has always evolved in response to global change. From sail to steam, and from coal to oil, each transformation has reshaped not only the ships that traverse our oceans but also the industries, ports, and communities that support them. Today, the sector stands at another defining moment. As the International Maritime Organization (IMO) advances its ambition to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, shipping is embarking on its most profound transformation in generations. Although international shipping currently accounts for around 3 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, these emissions could increase by up to 50 percent by 2050, depending on future economic and energy developments. Reversing this trajectory will require replacing or retrofitting thousands of vessels, developing entirely new fuel supply chains, and investing in port infrastructure at an unprecedented global scale.

The transition now underway is not simply an energy transition; it is an industrial transformation capable of reshaping maritime economies and creating new engines of sustainable growth.

It is tempting to view this challenge solely through the lens of decarbonisation. Cleaner fuels, new propulsion systems, and more efficient vessels understandably dominate public debate. Yet this captures only part of the opportunity. The transition now underway is not simply an energy transition; it is an industrial transformation capable of reshaping maritime economies and creating new engines of sustainable growth.

The countries that succeed will not necessarily be those that discover the next breakthrough technology. Rather, they will be those that build the most resilient maritime ecosystems.

From Decarbonisation to Industrial Transformation

The future competitiveness of the maritime sector will depend on far more than the fuel powering its ships. It will hinge on whether nations can integrate shipbuilding, ports, logistics, energy production, digital technologies, finance, education, and industrial innovation into coherent long-term strategies. The goal is not merely to operate greener ships, but to build stronger, more resilient maritime economies.

Shipbuilding illustrates this shift. While global production remains concentrated among a relatively small number of players, diversifying advanced shipbuilding capabilities would strengthen resilience and enable more countries to participate in the next generation of maritime manufacturing. Modern vessels already illustrate this evolution. For example, the dual-fuel container vessel Eco Levant, designed to operate on both conventional fuel and methanol, recently participated in the first-ever ethanol bunkering operation in the Port of Rotterdam. At the same time, AI-enabled voyage optimisation and advanced energy management systems are helping improve operational efficiency, demonstrating how ship design is becoming increasingly adaptable to future technological change. Shipowners are no longer investing solely in ships; they are investing in assets capable of adapting to decades of technological change.

The goal is not merely to operate greener ships, but to build stronger, more resilient maritime economies.

Encouragingly, this transition has already begun. Ocean-going vessels capable of operating on renewable and other alternative fuels are entering commercial service. According to DNV's Alternative Fuels Insight (AFI), hundreds of alternative-fuelled vessels are already in operation or on order, with methanol-capable ships representing one of the fastest-growing segments of the global fleet. Engine manufacturers continue to develop propulsion systems compatible with a growing range of alternative fuels, while ports have demonstrated commercial bunkering operations using new energy carriers. These milestones matter not because they validate a single technology, but because they demonstrate that innovation is moving decisively from concept to commercial implementation.

DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight (AFI) data reinforces what is already becoming clear: the future of shipping will almost certainly be multi-fuel. Different vessel types, operating profiles, and regional circumstances will require different solutions. Renewable liquid fuels, methanol/ethanol, ammonia, hydrogen, electricity, and technologies yet to emerge will each have a role according to technical, economic, and environmental considerations. Policymakers should therefore create technology-neutral frameworks that reward verified lifecycle emissions reductions while encouraging innovation across the full spectrum of sustainable solutions. This includes globally harmonised lifecycle greenhouse gas accounting methodologies under the IMO, fuel standards that reward emissions performance rather than prescribing specific technologies, and national policies that support investment in alternative-fuel production, bunkering infrastructure, and port development.

Yet fuels are only one component of a much larger picture. Alternative fuels require production facilities, storage terminals, distribution networks, bunkering infrastructure, trained personnel, safety standards, and new engineering capabilities. Every investment in maritime decarbonisation therefore stimulates activity well beyond shipping itself. Agriculture, renewable energy, manufacturing, logistics, research institutions, and financial services all become part of an interconnected value chain. This is where the true promise of the blue economy emerges.

Building Integrated Maritime Ecosystems

Too often, the blue economy is understood simply as economic activity taking place at sea. In reality, it is a development model that connects coastal infrastructure with inland industries, innovation with manufacturing, ports with communities, and environmental stewardship with long-term prosperity. Maritime development, therefore, extends far beyond harbours and shipping lanes into the wider economy.

Green ports illustrate this evolution particularly well. Traditionally viewed as gateways for cargo, ports are increasingly becoming integrated energy and industrial hubs. Examples include the Port of Rotterdam, which is expanding its role as a multi-fuel energy hub through alternative-fuel bunkering and industrial decarbonisation initiatives, and the Port of Singapore, which is advancing digitalisation while developing alternative-fuel and next-generation bunkering capabilities. Tomorrow's ports will increasingly accommodate multiple energy carriers, smart bunkering systems, digital logistics platforms, carbon accounting, circular recycling activities, and advanced maritime services. Around these facilities, engineering companies, equipment manufacturers, fuel suppliers, technology providers, training institutions, and research centres will develop. The result is not merely improved port performance, but dynamic industrial clusters that generate skilled employment, innovation, and long-term resilience.

Such ecosystems also strengthen national competitiveness. By developing local industrial capabilities, countries can strengthen supply chain resilience while creating opportunities for domestic enterprises to participate in global maritime value chains. Investments in shipbuilding, clean energy, port infrastructure, and maritime technologies reinforce one another, creating a virtuous cycle of innovation, capability development, and economic growth.

None of this transformation, however, will occur without partnership.

The Partnerships Powering the Maritime Transition

Shipping has always been a global industry. Ships routinely cross multiple jurisdictions within a single voyage, making fragmented regulatory approaches both costly and inefficient. The transition ahead will require international cooperation to develop common sustainability standards, transparent lifecycle greenhouse gas accounting, harmonised safety regulations, and innovative financing mechanisms capable of mobilising the substantial capital required for new vessels, port infrastructure, and clean energy production.

Accessible finance will be particularly important for emerging maritime economies. The transition must be both ambitious and inclusive. If sustainable technologies remain accessible only to the largest markets, the maritime sector risks creating new divides precisely when global collaboration is most needed. For many developing maritime economies, high capital costs, limited access to green finance, insufficient alternative-fuel infrastructure, and technology transfer remain significant barriers to participation in the transition. Fair access to investment, technology, and expertise must therefore be recognised as essential components of a successful maritime transition.

Progress is achieved not by advancing a single technology or fuel, but by creating the conditions in which innovation, investment and industrial partnerships can flourish together.

The Global Ethanol Association is helping build bridges between sectors that have traditionally operated independently. For instance, the Association fosters collaboration between agriculture, renewable energy producers, engine manufacturers, ports, shipowners, regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to create the integrated ecosystems required for maritime decarbonisation. This demonstrates that progress is achieved not by advancing a single technology or fuel, but by creating the conditions in which innovation, investment and industrial partnerships can flourish together.

History teaches that shipping has never prospered through isolation. It has flourished through connectivity, openness, and the continuous exchange of ideas, technologies, and commerce.

The greatest blue breakthrough of the coming decades will not be a single fuel, engine, or ship design. It will be the emergence of integrated maritime ecosystems that combine advanced shipbuilding, modern ports, diversified energy solutions, skilled people, resilient supply chains, and international cooperation into a coherent vision for sustainable growth.

Countries that embrace this broader perspective will achieve far more than cleaner shipping. They will build competitive maritime industries, stronger coastal economies, and a truly sustainable blue economy that delivers environmental progress alongside lasting prosperity.

That is the real opportunity before the maritime sector as a whole. It should be seized together.

Sylvain Zurcher is President and Co-founder, Global Ethanol Association.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The ARA divide
summary: Rotterdam's early RED III implementation has predictably driven conventional bunker demand to Antwerp, as shipowners simply seek cheaper HFO elsewhere. While Rotterdam boasts a doubling of biofuel blend sales to 240,000 tonnes in Q2 2026, this localized shift does little to curb overall carbon intensity when vessels simply bunker 100% fossil fuels at neighbouring ports. Such regulatory arbitrage undermines FuelEU Maritime goals, allowing high-emitting ships to avoid immediate fines by merely changing bunkering locations, not their fuel consumption.
content:
The ARA bunker market appears to be diverging, with conventional fuel demand gravitating towards Antwerp while Rotterdam leads in both alternative fuel volumes and fuel diversity.

Rotterdam’s conventional bunker market has come under pressure since the Netherlands implemented the revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) earlier this year, with the port trailing Antwerp in conventional bunker volumes for the second straight quarter.

Rotterdam’s conventional bunker market has come under pressure since the Netherlands implemented the revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) earlier this year, with the port trailing Antwerp in conventional bunker volumes for the second straight quarter.

The Port of Rotterdam attributed part of the decline in conventional fuel sales to the additional sustainability obligations imposed on fuel suppliers. The port authority said the measures have increased the cost of conventional bunker fuels relative to competing ports, prompting some shipowners to bunker elsewhere.

Rotterdam port association Deltalinqs and four other industry bodies made the same case in a position paper submitted to Dutch ministries on 20 July, arguing that differences in Dutch implementation of RED III have created an uneven playing field and shifted conventional bunker demand to neighbouring ports.

“The Netherlands’ early implementation of RED III was intended to accelerate the transition to greener fuels. In practice, however, the opposite is now happening: ships are simply bunkering 100% fossil fuels elsewhere,” Deltalinqs said.

While Rotterdam appears to be losing conventional bunker volumes to Antwerp, it continues to record significantly higher sales of low- and zero-emission bunker fuels than the latter.

Rotterdam’s biofuel blend sales more than doubled from around 105,000 mt in the first quarter to about 240,000 mt in the second quarter of 2026. A market source partly attributed the increase to biofuel’s improving economics against LSMGO amid higher fossil fuel prices during the Middle East war.

“The compression of bio-bunker premiums during the quarter, when biofuel premiums in relation to fossil marine fuel prices were shrinking, was also a supportive factor,” Prima Markets analyst Ulrich Arnheiter said.

Growth extended beyond biofuels

Bio-methanol deliveries almost tripled to around 3,000 mt, from about 1,000 mt in the first quarter.

Rotterdam recorded ethanol bunker sales for the first time in the second quarter, at around 1,000 mt. X-Press Feeders’ Eco Levant took an ethanol-methanol blend in May, and Maersk’s Laura Maersk followed with a larger barge delivery of 100% ethanol in June.

Only liquefied biomethane (LBM) volumes declined, with bunker sales falling to 3,000 mt from 7,000 mt in the previous quarter.

Across the border, Antwerp’s bio-bunker sales increased from around 21,000 mt to nearly 27,000 mt over the same period, but remained well below Rotterdam’s volumes. No methanol sales were reported in the port, which does not break out LBM volumes separately.

Suppliers in both Rotterdam and Antwerp offer biofuels, LBM and methanol. But the Dutch port’s position as one of the world’s largest bunker ports and Europe’s largest container port could make it a logical location to test emerging fuels, with a larger concentration of early-adopter shipowners, fuel suppliers and demonstration projects than its neighbouring ports.

Commercial factors including pricing, fuel availability, lead times, supplier offerings and shipowner procurement strategies are also likely to influence bunker purchasing decisions.

For instance, LSMGO-equivalent B100 can now be cheaper than LSMGO in Dutch ports once EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime incentives, and discounts from Dutch ZRE A tickets, are included in the price, Joe Tierney told ENGINE. Tierney is the head of trading at Verde Marine Energy.

The improved economics are driving a “huge increase in B100 demand and requirements”, he said.

At the same time, Rotterdam’s current lead does not necessarily mean the gap will persist going ahead.

For instance, Equinor is due to begin supplying Wallenius Wilhelmsen with bio-methanol in Antwerp and Zeebrugge from late 2026 under a two-year agreement. As suppliers expand availability of alternative fuels across the ARA region, differences in fuel availability and bunker sales between the region’s major hubs could narrow over time.

In other news this week, Brazil’s national energy agency has launched a public consultation on a draft resolution proposing to permit up to 100% biofuel (B100) for routine marine bunkering, law firm Mayer Brown said. The current regulation limits the biodiesel content of marine diesel oil to a maximum of 0.5% by volume.

The European Commission has approved a €103 million ($117 million) Dutch State aid scheme to support the deployment of methanol- and hydrogen-powered vessels. The funding will support both newbuilds and retrofits across multiple vessel types, including passenger and cargo ships, primarily for short-sea shipping.
